newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav economy not in recession - Tanjug. [CORRECTED 19:22 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav economy not in recession - Tanjug. [CORRECTED 19:22 GMT]

text.p: Stable prices and dinar exchange rate and moderate but continuous production and export growth in the first quarter of 1997 indicate the Yugoslav economy is not in recession, contrary to certain public assessments, Tanjug news agency said Wednesday.

"The best results in the first quarter were in the sector of prices because their cumulative growth was only three percent," Federal Statistics Office Director Milovan Zivkovic was quoted by the state news agency as saying.
According to Zivkovic, if this trend continues, total annual retail price growth will be between 12 and 15 percent.
"This would represent so-called carried-over inflation, which means inflation this year would be zero," he said.
The next "front" of stability in Q1 was the dinar, whose black market exchange rate has stabilized at 3.6 to the German mark, Zivkovic said.
The dinar plummetted to 4.3 early in January following a substantial increase in money supply in the last days of 1996.
Zivkovic said he expected the dinar's street value to continue stabilizing to 3.4 dinars to the mark. The official rate is 3.3 dinars to the mark.
But dinar and price stability will depend on whether monetary policy remains restrictive, as announced, he said.
Q1 cumulative industrial output growth of 6.5 percent against the same period 1996 is satisfactory in view of the conditions it was achieved in, Zivkovic said.

"Such results are important because they were achieved in the absence of European Union (EU) trade preferentials, under an invisible wall of sanctions and Yugoslavia's unresolved status in international financial and trade organisations."
Zivkovic forecast double digit industrial growth in the first six months of the year compared to the same period 1996.
He said export growth of 37.6 percent in the January-March period approached the 44 percent target for the year.

Although Yugoslavia was officially informed last month the EU had postponed for a year decisions on restoring trade preferentials, there are reliable signals the issue will be on the agenda of the EU Council of Ministers meeting later this month, Zivkovic said.

"There are also indications the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank will re-establish contacts with Yugoslavia in the second quarter, either in our country or on 'their territory'," he said.
